I've farmed these fields in Quzhou for more than forty years, and at sixty-five I know better than to gamble with new crops on the North China Plain. My five mu will stay in the wheat-maize double-cropping rotation that has always fed my family. The winter wheat is already in the ground from last autumn, and after we harvest it in early June, I will immediately plant summer maize—there is barely a week's window, so I never waste time with experiments. I buy improved wheat varieties and hybrid maize seeds from the county supply station because the yield stability matters more to me than saving a few yuan; one bad year at my age would hurt more than the seed cost. I keep fertilizer moderate—about fourteen to sixteen kilograms of nitrogen per mu—because I have seen how burning money on excess urea damages the soil and my wallet. I will run the pump for three irrigations on the wheat and two on the maize, and I spray when I have to: three times for wheat, twice for maize, mostly herbicide and fungicide. I use rotary tillage to get a clean seedbed fast, especially for the maize planting after wheat harvest. If the weather is fair, I expect roughly 550 kg per mu of wheat and 650 kg per mu of maize. It is not fancy, but it is honest income I can rely on.
